title: Loving a city to death
text: Venice has roughly 50,000 residents and, in a busy year, some 25 million visitors. The arithmetic {{1}} the problem: each tourist is welcome as an individual, and collectively they {{2}} the city they came to see. The symptoms repeat across the map: rental platforms {{3}} flats out of the housing market and into short lets, neighbourhood shops give way to souvenir outlets, and residents {{4}} the centre to the visitors. Cities have tried everything. Barcelona fined illegal rentals; Dubrovnik {{5}} cruise ships to two a day; Venice {{6}} an entry fee for day-trippers and banned large ships from the lagoon. The economics are genuinely {{7}}: tourism employment is real, and few cities can simply switch it off. The plausible {{8}} is management rather than bans — spreading visitors across seasons and districts, pricing access, and treating residents' daily life as infrastructure worth defending. The alternative is on display already: a postcard with nobody left in it to post it.

gaps.explanation: 'the arithmetic states the problem' — lays it out plainly; spell takes 'out' (spell out), steer = guide.
'collectively they consume the city' — use it up; assume = take for granted.
'platforms siphon flats out of the market' — drain them off, like liquid up a tube; sift = separate with a sieve.

gaps.hint: give up formally (___ the centre to)
gaps.explanation: 'residents cede the centre to the visitors' — formally surrender it; seethe = boil with suppressed anger.
'Dubrovnik capped cruise ships at two a day' — fixed a ceiling; cordon takes 'off'.
'Venice trailed an entry fee' — announced it before introducing it; tame = domesticate.
'the economics are genuinely awkward' — uncomfortable to deal with; arduous = requiring great effort.
'the plausible answer is management rather than bans' — the solution; antler = a deer's horn.
